expertInsight: The Business Analyst exam covers stakeholder work and discovery methods as well as Salesforce. About a third of my exam tested business analysis methods, such as elicitation, user stories, acceptance criteria, and backlog priorities when stakeholders disagree. Salesforce questions asked when to use configuration or code and how to turn business needs into data model choices. Study Agile and Scrum along with the platform. The passing score is 72%, one of the highest for consultant exams.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Business Analyst exam hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This is a moderately difficult exam with a high passing score. About half the exam covers business analysis, such as discovery and user stories. The other half tests Salesforce knowledge, including what the platform can do.
bullets: 72% to pass, or about 44 correct answers out of 60. This is higher than many consultant exams, so check the official exam guide before booking.
Business analysis methods matter. Expect questions on elicitation, process mapping, and user stories.
Use Salesforce wisely. Know when configuration can meet a need and when it requires custom development.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can plan a discovery session: who to speak with, which method to use, what to document, and how to get agreement. Aim for at least 85% on practice tests because the passing score is 72%.

examFormat.heading: Business Analyst exam format
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test center. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a project situation, such as stakeholders who disagree or a requirement that keeps changing. They ask what the analyst should do next.
bestWayToPass: Choose the right discovery method: Interviews, workshops, observation, surveys, and document review each help with different needs.
Write clear user stories: Include a role, goal, and benefit. Add acceptance criteria a tester can check.
Map the process first: Document the current process, then the future process, and list the gaps.
Know what Salesforce can do: Learn enough to tell whether a requirement is simple to configure, costly, or not possible.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers the Business Analyst role on Salesforce projects: discovering and recording requirements, writing user stories, mapping processes, working with stakeholders, and supporting testing and adoption. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 72% pass mark, weighted towards Collaboration with Stakeholders (23%) and Requirements (18%).

keyConcepts.h2: Business Analyst: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Discovery and Elicitation
blocks.body: You need to ask for requirements and learn how work is done. **Interviews** give you time to learn from one person, especially about sensitive topics. **Workshops** help a group discuss issues and agree on decisions. **Observation** means watching someone do the work; it can reveal steps they forget to mention. **Surveys** reach many people with simple questions, but you cannot ask follow-up questions. **Document analysis** and reviews of the current system show how work happens today. Choose the method based on whether you need detail, agreement, broad input, or evidence. Prepare questions, record decisions, and share your notes so people can correct anything you missed.

blocks.heading: User Stories and Acceptance Criteria
blocks.body: A **user story** states the user’s role, goal, and benefit. For example: “As a sales rep, I want to see a customer’s open cases on an opportunity so that I know about problems before a renewal call.” The benefit helps the team decide how important the story is. **Acceptance criteria** list what must be true for the story to be complete. They should be clear enough for a tester to check. Good stories are small enough for one work cycle and focus on the need, not a set design. A story about a screen layout may describe a solution before the team understands the need.

blocks.heading: Stakeholders and Getting Decisions Made
blocks.body: Projects often stall because people disagree. Map stakeholders by their **influence** and **interest**, then plan how to involve each group. Choose who can make decisions before conflicts come up. When people want different things, return to the business goal and what you learned during discovery; do not decide based only on job title. Keep a **RAID** record of risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies. Write assumptions down because hidden assumptions can lead to late surprises.

blocks.heading: Process Mapping and Gap Analysis
blocks.body: Map the **current state** before you design a solution. The real process often differs from how people describe it. Then map the **future state**. Compare the two to complete a **gap analysis** and identify work for the backlog. Keep process maps easy to read; swimlanes can show who does each step. Note when work moves from Salesforce to email or spreadsheets, where delays and errors can occur. A map also helps explain why a step was removed.

blocks.heading: Requirements, Testing and Adoption
blocks.body: Separate **functional** requirements, which describe what a system must do, from **non-functional** requirements such as speed, security, accessibility, and capacity. These are easy to miss and can be costly to add later. Use **traceability** to connect each business need to a story and a test. Plan **user acceptance testing** with real users who check the solution against the acceptance criteria. Then plan training, communication, and a way to measure whether people use the solution. A solution only helps if people use it.

scenarioTips.h2: How to pass the Salesforce Business Analyst exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions ask what the analyst should do next. The best answer usually helps the team understand the need or record an agreement before building a solution.

blocks.heading: Choosing an Elicitation Technique
blocks.body: Use an interview for detail or sensitive topics, a workshop to help a group agree, observation to learn what people really do, and a survey to ask simple questions of many people.

blocks.heading: User Stories
blocks.body: Include the role, goal, benefit, and acceptance criteria a tester can check. If a story describes a screen instead of a need, it may jump to a solution too soon.

blocks.heading: Process Mapping
blocks.body: Map the current process first, then the future process, then identify the gap. Swimlanes show who does each step and where work leaves Salesforce.

blocks.heading: Testing
blocks.body: Users run user acceptance testing against the acceptance criteria. A project team demo is not UAT.

blocks.heading: Stakeholders
blocks.body: Map stakeholder influence and interest, name decision-makers early, and use business goals and discovery evidence to resolve disagreements.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Consultant Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Business Analyst:

sampleQuestions.question: What does a Certified Business Analyst do on a Salesforce project?
options: Learn what the business needs, document requirements, and work with stakeholders
Manage the server infrastructure, monitor uptime, and apply patches to the production org
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Certified Business Analyst learns the business needs, records the requirements, and works with stakeholders to shape Salesforce solutions that improve the business.
whyWrong: Writing Apex is a developer task, not the main focus of a Business Analyst.
Designing email campaigns is a Marketing task, not business analysis.
Managing server infrastructure is an IT operations task, not business analysis.

sampleQuestions.question: Which method is often used to learn and document business requirements?
options: Deployment scripts reviewed with the release manager
sampleQuestions.explanation: Stakeholder interviews and workshops help discover and document business requirements.
whyWrong: Deployment scripts are used for releases, not requirements discovery.
API development is an implementation task, not requirements discovery.
Unit testing is a software testing task, not requirements discovery.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a Business Analyst usually prepare before development starts?
options: A requirements document and user stories
A deployed package in the production environment
sampleQuestions.explanation: Business Analysts prepare requirements documents and user stories to guide development.
whyWrong: Test classes are written for software testing; they are not the Business Analyst’s usual pre-development deliverable.
Integration code is built during implementation, not requirements gathering.
A deployed package is a release artifact created after development.

sampleQuestions.question: How should a Business Analyst prioritize requirements that conflict?
options: Use business goals and agreement among stakeholders
Always choose the option the technical team finds easiest
sampleQuestions.explanation: Priorities should support business goals and have stakeholder agreement.
whyWrong: Leaving every decision to IT avoids the Business Analyst’s role in helping stakeholders agree.
Always choosing the technical option ignores business goals and stakeholder needs.
Choosing the least expensive option may ignore business goals and stakeholder needs.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Salesforce project artifact turns business needs into features the team can build?
options: A legacy Process Builder automation diagram
sampleQuestions.explanation: User stories and acceptance criteria describe business needs as clear features the team can build.
whyWrong: A deployment checklist is used to manage a release, not to turn requirements into features.
Process Builder is a legacy automation tool, not a requirements document.
A debug log helps troubleshoot technical issues; it does not define features.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the common format for an Agile user story?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The common format is “As a [role], I want [goal] so that [benefit].” It states who needs a feature, what they need, and why.
whyWrong: This is not the common Agile user story format.
Given/When/Then is a Gherkin or BDD format used for acceptance criteria, not the user story itself.
“The system shall” is a traditional way to write a requirement, not the common Agile user story format.

sampleQuestions.question: What do acceptance criteria define for a user story?
options: The specific conditions that must be met for the story to be complete
The technical design the development team must use to build the story
The expected performance measures for the solution
sampleQuestions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are pass-or-fail conditions that show whether a user story is complete. They tell the product owner what to check and help prevent rework caused by unclear expectations.
whyWrong: Acceptance criteria define what the story must do, not how developers should build it.
Dependencies and risks are usually documented separately.
Performance measures are non-functional requirements, not the main purpose of acceptance criteria.

sampleQuestions.question: A Business Analyst records the current steps in a process before designing a new solution. What is this called?
options: Requirements traceability across stories and tests
sampleQuestions.explanation: As-Is analysis documents how the process works today. It helps find problems and gaps before designing the future To-Be process.
whyWrong: Solution validation checks whether a built solution meets needs.
Stakeholder mapping identifies people involved and their influence.
Requirements traceability links requirements to things such as tests.

sampleQuestions.question: Which method helps a Business Analyst compare stakeholders’ influence and interest in a project?
options: Process decomposition into smaller sub-process diagrams
Stakeholder analysis with a Power/Interest Grid
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Power/Interest Grid maps stakeholders by their influence and interest. It helps decide whether to manage them closely, keep them satisfied, keep them informed, or monitor them.
whyWrong: Process decomposition breaks a process into steps.
Gap analysis compares current and desired states.
User story mapping shows how stories fit into a user journey.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a Requirements Traceability Matrix used for on a Salesforce project?
options: Mapping database tables to Salesforce objects
Recording each role and permission level in the org, with the users assigned to them
Linking each business requirement to related user stories, features, and tests
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Traceability Matrix links requirements to user stories and tests. This helps confirm that every requirement is built and tested.
whyWrong: Mapping tables to objects is part of data architecture.
Role and permission levels are part of access control.
Deployment history is part of release management.

sampleQuestions.question: A team finds that its solution misses some original business requirements. Which Business Analyst method can help identify this gap?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Gap analysis compares the current or planned solution with the desired future state. It shows which requirements are still unmet.
whyWrong: A process flow diagram shows process steps.
A risk register tracks project risks.
A RACI chart defines roles and responsibilities.

sampleQuestions.question: Which requirement type describes performance, security, usability, or scalability rather than a specific feature?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe quality attributes, or how a system works. Examples include page load time, concurrent user capacity, and data security.
whyWrong: Functional requirements describe what a system does.
Technical specifications describe implementation details, not this broader type of quality measure.
Business requirements describe high-level business needs.

sampleQuestions.question: In a discovery workshop, two business units give conflicting requirements for the same field. What should the Business Analyst do first?
options: Use the version requested by the most senior stakeholder and close the question there
Ask the project manager to decide
Record both requests and lead a follow-up meeting to agree on one requirement
sampleQuestions.explanation: Record the conflicting requests and help stakeholders resolve them in a structured discussion. This surfaces why each unit needs the field and helps build agreement.
whyWrong: Choosing the senior person’s request without discussion may leave the other unit’s needs unresolved.
Escalating immediately skips the Business Analyst’s role in helping stakeholders work through the conflict.
Choosing the simpler option may ignore the business need behind either request.

sampleQuestions.question: In Salesforce project governance, what does the DACI framework define?
options: Deployment steps across sandbox, staging, and production
The order of automation steps in approval processes and record-triggered flows
Decision-making roles: Driver, Approver, Contributor, and Informed
The data architecture for objects, fields, and relationships
sampleQuestions.explanation: DACI clarifies who drives a decision, who approves it, who contributes, and who needs to be informed.
whyWrong: DACI is a decision-making framework, not a deployment plan.
DACI is for decision roles, not automation design.
DACI is for decision roles, not data architecture.

sampleQuestions.question: What format do user stories usually follow in Salesforce projects?
options: As a [role], I want [goal] so that [benefit]
As a [system], I want [data] so that [report]
sampleQuestions.explanation: User stories usually follow this format: “As a [role], I want [goal] so that [benefit].” It connects the user, the feature, and its business value.
whyWrong: This is not the common user story format, which focuses on role, goal, and benefit.
This is too specific to one example and is not the common user story format.
A user story usually describes a human role, not the system itself.
